title: The fake Microsoft support call
notes: Format "Was tust du?" (Format-Bibel 1.0), Reihe "Was tust du?". F1 EN (localised from the DE spec). Example case staged: firm, caller, times and sequence are invented; Microsoft only appears as the impersonated name, the way Microsoft itself describes the scam. Mechanism and step from S1 and S2, re-read 02.11.2026. No emergency step, because the sources' text names none. The old plan ai_security-20261114-1-en.json stays unchanged.

layout.description: A friendly caller from 'Microsoft support' wants access to your computer. What do you do? A staged case with three answers and the one step Microsoft and Germany's BSI advise.

unverified: The old plan's lines on spoofed caller ID, money for an unneeded fix and payment in cryptocurrency or gift cards are no longer in the text of the Microsoft page on 02.11.2026 (now 'Protect yourself from online scams and attacks'): not used.
The sequence of the example case (times, slow PC, the caller's requests) is invented and marked as an example.

That a name and staff number (option B) prove nothing is Scutoria's interpretation of S2 (deception about identity); marked as interpretation on screen. 'Your own IT provider' stands for Microsoft's 'trusted advisor'.
Emergency steps after granting remote access: Microsoft only points to a video, not used.

hook_candidates.spoken: Microsoft calls: your computer has errors. What do you do?
A call from Microsoft support must be real? Microsoft doesn't cold call.
Genuine Microsoft error messages never include a phone number.
hook_candidates.on_screen: Error message with a hotline? Never

hook_candidates.spoken: One call from 'support', and a stranger is controlling your computer.
Tuesday, 10:47 a.m. Microsoft support is on the phone.
hook_candidates.visual: clock, the incoming call arrives as a paper card, the request for remote access is marked

beats.spoken: Tuesday, 10:47 a.m. The phone rings. A friendly man from Microsoft support: We can see errors on your PC. Please install a program for remote access.

mail.subject: Errors on your PC
lines: We can see errors on your PC.

beats.spoken: You listen carefully. The name: Microsoft. The tone: calm and competent. The problem: sounds possible, your PC really is slow. All plausible. But Microsoft says it itself: unless you contact it first, Microsoft won't call you to offer support.

fact.text: Microsoft won't call you to offer support unasked.

beats.spoken: What do you do? A: You allow access, but watch closely. B: You ask for his name and staff number. C: You hang up and call your own IT provider. Remember your choice.

options.text: Ask for name and staff number
Hang up, call your own IT

beats.spoken: Let's play out A. The program runs, and he controls your computer. You watch as he shows you so-called errors. Then he wants your password. According to Microsoft, scammers steal information or install malware while they do this.

The right answer is C. Microsoft advises: hang up on unsolicited support calls, and if you're worried about your device, call someone you trust. Germany's BSI adds: never give out passwords on the phone. A hands him the computer. B proves nothing, names are easy to invent.

card.title: Hang up, call your own IT
card.sub: remote access only for your own IT

strikes.text: B: Ask for name and number

sources.label: BSI · no passwords on the phone

beats.spoken: An unexpected support call? Hanging up is allowed. What would you have picked? Tell me in the comments.
